title: Shopping cart requirements
idea: Scoping a shopping cart means naming who uses it, what they can do, the rule that must never break, and what v1 leaves out.
points: Shoppers browse products, edit a cart, check out, pay, and cancel orders.
The core rule: never sell more units than the warehouse holds.
Stock is reserved at checkout, not when an item enters a cart.
Assume many cart edits, few checkouts, and spikes during sales.

edges.caption: The shopper starts on product pages that show price and whether stock exists.
Adding to the cart only records intent. No stock is taken yet.
Checkout reprices every line and reserves stock for all lines, or for none.
Payment turns the order PAID. The reservation becomes a real stock deduction.
A shopper may cancel before shipping. Stock goes back and money is refunded.

edges.label: expires
edges.caption: The system is an actor too: it releases stock held by orders nobody paid for.
Returns, catalog admin screens and search wait for a later version. Say so out loud.

code.title: Use cases as an enum
code.caption: The scope written as code: every use case names its actor, and v1 is an explicit set.

walk.text: v1 is a named set. A use case not in it is out of scope.
Print every use case with an IN or OUT tag and its actor.
Count v1 use cases per actor. An `EnumMap` keeps the order stable.
Three actors: the shopper, the system itself, and an admin.
Six use cases form the buying path, including stock release by the system.
Catalog admin, returns and recommendations are listed, so the cut is visible.

pitfalls: Do not reserve stock on add-to-cart; idle carts would lock up the whole catalog.
State traffic numbers as assumptions; never present a guess as a measured fact.
Forgetting the system actor hides the release of unpaid stock until late.

quiz.q: When should the design take stock away from other shoppers?
options: When the item is added to a cart
When the order ships from the warehouse
At checkout, as a reservation with an expiry
Never; check stock only after payment
quiz.why: Reserving at checkout protects the paying shopper for a short time. Earlier locks out browsers; later lets two people pay for one unit.

takeaway: Agree on actors, use cases and the no-overselling rule before designing.

starters: Should guest carts without login be in v1 scope?
How long should a checkout reservation last?
Which scale assumptions should I state for a cart in an interview?
